newsitem.title: POLAND: Lithuania seeks closer parliament link with Poland.
newsitem.headline: Lithuania seeks closer parliament link with Poland.

text.p: Lithuania's parliamentary leader Vytautas Landsbergis invited Poland's legislature on Friday to set up a permanent joint body for considering matters of mutual interest, such as European integration.

In a speech to Poland's lower house, delivered largely in Polish, Landsbergis recalled the link between the neighbours which centuries ago formed a single commonwealth and said they should put aside any differences to pursue common goals.
Landsbergis, who led Lithuania's struggle to quit the Soviet Union in 1991, proposed talks on setting up an institutionalised structure for regular consultation and long-term cooperation.
"If we created a permanent Polish-Lithuanian inter-parliamentary institution, we could arrange many matters more efficiently without unnecessary delay," he said.
"Its voice would carry further, as the common voice of two countries, than individual voices," he told the parliamentarians, who repeatedly applauded his speech.
Landsbergis later told a news conference that such a body might consist of 20 delegates from each country's legislature, but it was up to the two parliaments to work out details.
He said the parliaments could also decide to what extent standpoints agreed by these delegates would be regarded as official policies of the two countries.
"I think it would be good if they met at least every three months," Landsbergis said.
Like Poland, which escaped Soviet domination in 1989, Lithuania wants to join the European Union and NATO quickly.

It has an association agreement with the EU, but is much further from NATO than Poland, which expects to join by 1999, largely because Russia even more adamantly opposes the three Baltic states' membership of the pact than that of Poland.
There has sometimes been tension between Poland and Lithuania over issues including treatment of each other's minorities.
In the early 1990s Lithuania focused on finding allies in Scandinavia rather than Poland, which before World War Two included within its borders the Lithuanian capital Vilnius.
Landsbergis said Poland had grown warmer and was now very friendly towards Lithuania.

Poland's lower house speaker, Jozef Zych, said the offices of both parliaments would work on a plan for bilateral cooperation and in the meanwhile the two speakers would dispense with all formalities and meet whenever they liked but certainly not less than once every three months.
